extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys/agents, patentees, and patent office practitioners (United Kingdom)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the statutory and procedural standards for the grant, duration, territorial effect, correction, and amendment (disclaimer/correction/explanation) of UK patents and the practice and grounds for opposition and judicial orders concerning amendments under the Patents Acts (chiefly 1883 and 1888).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller's power to refuse grant (contrary to law or morality) (s.86 Patents Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the eighty-sixth section of the Patents Act of 1883 the Comptroller may refuse to grant a patent for an invention the use of which would, in his opinion, be contrary to law or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an express discretionary ground for refusal; the Comptroller evaluates whether proposed use would offend law or morality. No examples beyond the statutory text are given in this chunk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial effect of a patent (s.16 Patents Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent when sealed shall have effect throughout the United Kingdom and the Isle of Man, leaving out the Channel Islands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent rights are territorially limited as specified by statute; check whether special territories are excluded or included by later legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent duration (s.17 Patents Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of every patent is limited to fourteen years from its date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time runs from the day of the date of the patent, including that day (cases such as Russell v. Ledsam). See Chapter XIV for extension procedures and Privy Council principles on prolongation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent form and single-invention principle (s.33 Act of 1888)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent may be in the prescribed form, and a patent is to be granted for one invention only (s.33), although no objection in proceedings can be taken that it comprises more than one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board of Trade may alter the form; while the statute nominally limits patents to one invention, objections on multiplicity are not grounds in later actions/ proceedings under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents and effect of the letters patent (form of grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crown grants the patentee licence, full power and sole privilege to make/use/exercise/vend the invention during the term, and commands subjects not to infringe, but the grant is void if contrary to law, prejudicial to subjects, not new as to public use within the UK, or if the patentee is not the first and true inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant confers exclusive rights but subject to statutory nullifying provisos; review facts on novelty, true inventorship and public use to assess validity of the grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voidance of grant for non-payment of fees or failure to supply for Crown service
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant is made void if the patentee fails to pay all fees required by law or fails to supply articles of the invention required for the service of the Crown on reasonable terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory conditions: fees and supply obligations are essential; failure to comply can render a patent void. Specifics on Crown supply terms are set by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribed payment schedule and annual fees (s.17 provisions and Appendix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments: a payment of £50 must be made before the end of the fourth year and £100 before the end of the eighth year (or adjusted for older patents); alternatively annual fees may be paid. Appendix and Patents Rules 1890 set amounts and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the precise sums and years applicable to the filing date; consult rules 45–48 for certificates of payment/renewal procedure and Appendix for full fee schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlargement of time for late payments (Comptroller discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, by accident, mistake, or inadvertence, a patentee fails to make a prescribed payment in time, he may apply to the Comptroller for enlargement of time; the Comptroller, satisfied of the cause and on receipt of prescribed fee (not exceeding £10), may enlarge time but not for more than three months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow rule 49 Patents Rules 1890 and form K for procedure; enlargement is discretionary and limited to three months. Timely application and payment of the enlargement fee are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to pay on damages in infringement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an infringement occurs after failure to make a prescribed payment and before enlargement, the Court may, if it thinks fit, refuse to award any damages in respect of such infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-payment can affect remedies available in subsequent suits; parties should be aware that courts may deny damages for infringement committed in such lapsed periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment deadline exceptions for holidays/weekends
rubrics_metrics.description: When the last day for paying a fee falls on Christmas Day, Good Friday, Saturday, Sunday, a Bank holiday, or a day observed as public fast or thanksgiving, the fee may be paid on the next day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory accommodation for public holidays; compute deadlines accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost or destroyed patent — duplication (s.37)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent is lost or destroyed, or non-production is satisfactorily accounted for to the Comptroller, he may cause a duplicate to be sealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller has power to issue duplicate patents on satisfactory proof; follow the statutory procedure for applying for duplicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of clerical errors in letters patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerical errors in Letters Patent may be corrected by the Master of the Rolls (historically) or by the Comptroller under section 18 of the Patents Act 1883; applications for correction must be made within a reasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply promptly; case law (Re Nickel's Patent, He Garrett, Adam's Patent) indicates jurisdiction and timing considerations. Use Comptroller amendment powers where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crown use and compulsory licences (pre- and post-1883 distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crown historically had a right to free use of patented inventions (R v Leather) for patents before the Act of 1883; patents granted after the Act are to have the same effect against the Crown as against subjects (s.27), with statutory provisions for use subject to Treasury-approved terms or settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check grant date relative to 1883 to determine Crown rights; for post-1883 patents Crown use is subject to compensation/agreement procedures and possible compulsory licence provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of State for War's power over munitions inventions (s.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: By s.44 of the Patents Act 1883 the Secretary of State for War may acquire by purchase or gift the benefit of inventions/improvements in munitions of war and any patent obtained for the same, and may prevent disclosure of such inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military-sensitive inventions may be acquired or restricted from disclosure under statutory powers — check applicability for munitions-related patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for true and first inventor against fraudulent applications (s.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: By s.35 a patent granted to the true and first inventor is not to be invalidated by an application in fraud of him, by provisional protection obtained thereon, or by any use or publication of the invention subsequent to the fraudulent application during the period of provisional protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory protection shields bona fide first inventors from certain prior fraudulent filings; analyze chain of application dates and facts of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of statute repeals on prior patents (s.113 and transitional rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: S.113 repeals specified statutes but provides that repeal shall not affect the past operation of those statutes; interplay with earlier s.25 (Patents Act 1852) and s.45 of 1883 affects whether British patents become void by reason of related foreign patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional and retrospective effects are complex; cases (Singer v. Stassen, Brandon's Patent, A'Court v. Gardner) interpret whether earlier statutory invalidating effects survive repeal — analyze dates and prior operations carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patentees' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is granted to two or more persons, each may use the invention without being liable to account to the other, subject to specific case law on trusteeship (Mathers v. Green; Hancock v. Dewley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership structure (tenants in common, trustees) may alter consequences; examine the grant wording and relevant precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of patentee's interest on death or bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee dies intestate before expiration, his interest passes to his personal representatives (not heir); in bankruptcy the property in the patent passes to the trustee or assignee like other personal assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent rights are personal property and follow estate/bankruptcy rules; plan assignments or estate arrangements accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to apply to amend specification (s.18(1) Patents Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant or patentee may from time to time, by request in writing left at the Patent Office, seek leave to amend his specification, including drawings, by way of disclaimer, correction, or explanation, stating the nature of such amendment and his reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal written application required; must describe the amendment and give reasons. Drawings can be amended. Use prescribed forms and comply with rules 52–59 Patents Rules 1890.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement of proposed amendments and opposition period (s.18(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The request and nature of the proposed amendment shall be advertised in the prescribed manner, and at any time within one month from its first advertisement any person may give notice at the Patent Office of opposition to the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the statutory advertisement process and one-month opposition window; failure to advertise properly may vitiate the procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller's hearing and appeal to law officer (s.18(3),(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where notice of opposition is given the Comptroller shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and shall hear and decide the case subject to an appeal to the law officer. If leave is refused by the Comptroller the applicant may appeal to the law officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller conducts initial hearing; law officer is appellate fact-finder and can hear parties and impose conditions. Follow rules governing appeals and hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law officer's hearing powers and finality in certain respects (s.18(4),(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: The law officer shall, if required, hear the person making the request and the person giving notice, determine whether and subject to what conditions the amendment ought to be allowed, and may make an order accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law officer can examine witnesses (rules appended) and make orders; in some circumstances there is no further appeal from the law officer's order on allowance/refusal of leave (case law noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on amendments that enlarge or materially vary claimed invention (s.18(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification, as amended, claim an invention substantially larger than or substantially different from the invention claimed by the specification as it stood before amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a central statutory limit. Comptroller and law officers must ensure amendments do not extend scope; where question is doubtful, amendment may be allowed 'at the patentee's peril.' Cases: Math and Frost, Lake's Patent, Van Gelders Patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive nature of leave to amend (s.18(9))
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to amend is conclusive as to the right to make the allowed amendment except in case of fraud; the amendment shall in all Courts and for all purposes be deemed to form part of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once allowed (and absent fraud) the amendment is effective across courts; check for allegations of fraud if third parties seek to challenge the amendment's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18 not available during pending infringement or revocation proceedings (s.18(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions permitting amendment under s.18 do not apply while an action for infringement or a proceeding for revocation is pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees engaged in litigation cannot apply directly under s.18 but can seek court orders under s.19 to permit application to the Patent Office (see s.19 procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure rules for amendments (Patents Rules 1890, rr.52–59)
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure on applications for amendments is regulated by rules 52–59 of the Patents Rules, 1890; amendments of published specifications must proceed under s.18; other amendments prior to acceptance are under ss.7 and 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the cited rules and Appendix forms (rule 58, form K, rule 59 advertising) for detailed practice, filing requirements, and office copy obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller's option regarding titles and provisional omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an applicant desires prior to acceptance of his complete specification to omit part of the invention covered by the original title, the Comptroller should give him the option of filing with the original title and insert clause or should amend the original title and provisional specification under ss.7 and 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller has administrative flexibility pre-acceptance; choose the route (retain title or amend) that best preserves the filing position and conforms with statutory powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is entitled to oppose where amended specification is same as a prior patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the ground of opposition is that the invention as described in the amended specification is the same as that comprised in a prior patent, it is not competent for any member of the public to oppose; the opponent must show that he has an interest in the prior patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only parties with a vested interest in the prior patent may oppose on identity grounds (e.g., owners, assignees). Cases: Beck's Patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated grounds of opposition to amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical grounds: the proposed amendment will introduce disconformity between provisional and complete specification; the scope of the invention will be enlarged; the amended specification will claim an invention substantially different from the original; the invention will be made the same as one described in a prior specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents should identify which statutory or equitable harm arises; narrowing amendments (restriction) are generally not valid grounds if the narrower invention remains covered by the original specification (cases cited: Cochrane, Ashworth, Nordenfelt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good/Bad grounds: narrowing by amendment is permitted when still covered
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a good ground of opposition that the invention will be restricted within narrower limits by the amendment, provided that the invention so restricted is covered by the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where narrowing was allowed: Cochrane's, Ashworth's, Nordenfelt's Patents. Opponents should show expansion or substantive change, not mere restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions historically imposed on allowing amendments (old law practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the old law (Act of 5 & 6 Wm. IV) law officers commonly imposed, as a condition of leave to amend, that no action for infringement before the date of the disclaimer should be brought against certain persons or the public; they sometimes required undertakings and verified lists of prior machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice provides precedent for protective conditions (e.g., Re Tranter's Patent, Newton's case); whether similar conditions are imposed under the 1883 Act depends on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions under Act of 1883 and 1888 practice (limiting retrospective effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 1883/1888 practice the law officer sometimes imposed conditions that no action should be brought in respect of infringements prior to a given date (e.g., Jan 1, 1884) to confine scope of retrospective relief; special circumstances may still induce conditions exempting past infringement claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical terms include barring claims for past infringements, barring amended specification from being receivable in evidence in pending actions, and allocation of costs. Cases: Hearson's, Westinghouse, Allen's, Ashworth's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and limits of an 'explanation' amendment under s.18
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'explanation' is intended to explain more clearly what was necessary to understand the patentee's meaning at the time he patented the invention; it is not intended to add subsequently acquired knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'explanation' to clarify original disclosure, correct misdescriptions (e.g., description of drawings), but avoid introducing new technical matter that postdates the filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court/judge power to allow application to amend during litigation (s.19 Act of 1888)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an action for infringement or proceeding for revocation the Court or a judge may order that the patentee be at liberty, subject to such terms as to costs and otherwise, to apply at the Patent Office for leave to amend his specification by disclaimer, and may direct postponement of trial; an office copy of the judge's order must be left with the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use s.19 to obtain a judge's order permitting s.18 application during litigation; terms often protect the defendant and trial may be stayed while the Patent Office considers the request (rule 58 compliance required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion and terms imposed by courts when granting liberty to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The court's discretion under s.19 is absolute in each case and will not be easily interfered with; terms imposed should give full protection to the other party (e.g., costs allocation, barring amended spec from evidence, confining action to amended spec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law exemplifies common terms: plaintiffs bear costs of amendment motion and defendants' costs up to the motion, amended specification not receivable in the action, no evidence of pre-amendment infringement, or confinement of action to amended spec (Singer v. Stassen, Codd v. Braiby, Fusee Vesta Co. v. Bryant & May).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consideration: discontinue action and apply at Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Given terms usually imposed when seeking court liberty to apply, it may sometimes save time and money to discontinue the action, apply for leave to amend at the Patent Office in the ordinary way, and then bring a fresh action if desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider strategic choice between pursuing an in-action amendment (with likely protective terms) and discontinuing to use normal Patent Office amendment procedures to secure a cleaner amendment record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of decision-makers to prevent scope extension; permitting doubtful amendments at patentee's peril
rubrics_metrics.description: It is part of the duty of the Comptroller and the law officers, when hearing applications for leave to amend, to see that the proposed amendment does not extend the scope of the patent or alter the claims so that the invention would become substantially larger or different; when the question is doubtful, the amendment ought to be allowed at the patentee's peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If clearly extending scope the amendment must be disallowed (Math and Frost); if doubtful, allowance is possible but risky (Lake's Patent). Challenges can be made in court if the amendment contravenes s.18(8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on altering claims and severing claims by disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer may sever and reject claims to subordinate parts where specification claims both a general combination and subordinate parts, but a specification cannot be altered to claim a combination or parts if they were not previously claimed; cannot strike out an entire claim and insert another claim to a subordinate part if original contained a distinct specific claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers can narrow but not introduce new claim scope; ensure sufficient matter remains to support the patent (Gaulard & Gibbs, United Horseshoe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting down broad method claims to a particular method
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a claim to all methods of effecting a certain result, it may be cut down by disclaimer to the particular method described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disclaimer to restrict overbroad method claims to the described embodiment where appropriate (Ashworth's Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction under old statute: disclaimer must not extend exclusive right
rubrics_metrics.description: Under earlier Acts, disclaimers were disallowed if they would extend the exclusive right granted by the letters patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical restriction emphasises that disclaimers must not broaden exclusivity; modern tests under s.18(8) maintain similar substance-focused limits.
